newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea to probe lawmakers in Hanbo scandal.
newsitem.headline: South Korea to probe lawmakers in Hanbo scandal.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors will summon for questioning on Friday three prominent lawmakers named by the founder of the stricken Hanbo Group as taking his money, a prosecution official said.
Among them is Kim Deog-ryong, a leading lawmaker of the ruling New Korea Party and a member of President Kim Young-sam's inner circle, the official said on Thursday.

Hanbo founder Chung Tae-soo said money was also delivered to Kim Sang-hyun, a senior lawmaker with the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, and Kim Yong-hwan, secretary-general of the United Liberal Democrats.
In testimony broadcast live from a Seoul jail on Monday, Chung told a parliamentary inquiry his aides gave money to the three politicians.
After the hearing, all three politicians denied taking money from Chung.
The prosecutors charged that Chung had bribed politicians and bankers to keep loans rolling into Hanbo's steelmaking flagship, which collapsed in January.
They alleged that Chung diverted millions of dollars from the bank loans earmarked for investment and used it to buy influence.
Chung is on trial on bribery and other charges along with nine others, including three associates of President Kim, in connection with the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co.

Hanbo expanded rapidly under Kim Young-sam's administration. But the collapse of its steelmaking flagship uncovered a tangled web of corruption that rocked the economy and devastated the president's image.
The prosecutors plan to later question 30 other people that Chung said he had given money to as "political funds or gifts", the official said. The prosecution declined to name the 30.
Of the total, 20 are members of parliament -- 13 from the ruling party, four from the National Congress, two from the United Liberal Democrats and one from the Democratic Party.
"We have decided to summon all people in the Chung Tae-soo list to clear up public doubts," the official said.
The opposition has attacked an earlier probe by prosecutors as a whitewash that failed to bring major players to justice.
In the parliamentary hearing, Chung also said he had donated money to President Kim's election campaign, but denied making personal payments to Kim.
Chung said his campaign contributions were legal because he was a member of the ruling party's finance committee.
He added that he gave up to one billion won ($1.12 million) to the ruling party, some of it to fund the 1992 presidential election.
